title: It fits
hookLine: eyes fit light and seasons fit crops, he argues, as signs of providence (Discourses 1.6)
last: NOT MORE BOOKS — SHOW ME HOW YOU ACT.

cards: Hold up your hand and look at it. Your eye is doing something remarkable right now: catching light that bounced off your skin and turning it into a hand.
But the eye alone would be useless in a dark room, and light alone, with no eye, would show nothing to anyone. Neither one makes sense alone. Together, you see a hand.
Epictetus noticed that, and built a whole chapter on it.

teach.b: Discourses book one, chapter six, is called on providence. To see it, Epictetus says, a person needs two things: the ability to take in everything that happens, and a grateful heart.
Without gratitude, you'll see the same world and only complain. Then he builds his case from things that fit.

teach.h: EYE AND LIGHT FIT EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Sight would be worth nothing if there were no colors and no light to see them by. Who made the one to match the other? And it isn't just the eye.
There's the mind, which takes what the senses bring and sorts it, compares it, draws conclusions. That fits too.

For the Stoics this fit is a sign that the world is ordered by reason, and that's what they mean by providence: not a God who fixes your parking tickets, but an intelligence woven through how things are made.
People have argued about this for a long time. In Epictetus' own day, the Epicureans said the world came together by chance.
Today some explain the fit between eye and light by evolution, some see design in it, and some see both. Epictetus' practical point doesn't wait for that argument to be settled.
He ends the chapter by turning it inward: you, too, were fitted for something.
You were given strength to bear what happens: patience, courage, a large spirit. So instead of crying that life is too hard, he says, notice what you were built to meet it with.

how: Some readers pair this chapter with a short gratitude practice: noticing one ordinary fit in the world, like eye and light, and one inner strength suited to the day's difficulty.

games.q: you're one of Epictetus' students, and life feels too heavy. what does chapter 1.6 tell you to do?
o: notice the strength you were given to meet it.
wait for the gods to fix it.
games.why: he says we were given patience, courage and a large spirit, so instead of crying, notice what we were built to meet life with.

practice: Let your eyes rest on something near you and notice one fit: the breath and the air, your hand and the cup it holds, the chair and the shape of you sitting in it. Stay with it for a few breaths.
Then ask, gently: what have I been given that fits today's hard thing? Patience, humor, a friend, a little stubbornness.

wordCard.voice: It fits. Epictetus' way into providence: eye and light, mind and world, and our own strength matched to what we have to bear.

orig.note: Greek pronoia: providence, literally 'forethought'; the title word of Discourses 1.6.
